grade.why: Pictured: a picture on the Images tab shows it.

construction.note: Three statements, two of them in Andreas: 'a log house occupied as a store by John Stephen Coates' Hogan', 'a small log building near the corner of Lake and South Water streets', and Currey's 'a log building about where South Water street intersects Lake street'. No source describes the corner treatment, the chinking or whether any of it was sided; the archetype builds hewn log, which is the commonest construction at the forks in 1835 and what all three descriptions name.

stories.note: Not stated. Andreas calls it 'a small log building' and gives it a 20 ft depth, and the two passages describing its use divide it side by side — a post office on one side and a store on the other — rather than by floor. A single-pen log building of this depth is single-storey by type at the forks in 1835. Inference from the type and the description, not from a statement.

wall_height_m.note: No figure is attested. 2.5 m is about 8 ft: one storey of hewn log wall at typical period course counts, plus a sill. What is inferred is that the wall height falls in this range, not that it is exactly 2.5 m — the same reading, and the same number, this project gives the Walker meeting house, which is the other single-storey log building it models.

roof_type.note: Not attested. Gable is the near-universal roof form for log construction of this type, period and region, and it is the form a 45 ft building of this depth is roofed with unless something says otherwise.

roof_pitch_deg.note: No pitch is attested. 35 degrees is the archetype's mid-range for a low single-storey log building roofed in riven shakes. Inferred from construction practice, not measured.

front_set_out.note: One sash between the visible gable corner and an off-centre doorway in Cameron's retrospective picture. Stations 8.45 m and 11.55 m run from minimum-u on the retained attested 13.716 m frontage. They were revised after actual paired renders exposed the first estimates too far along the wall. These are reconstructed positions under a provisional six-wallpoint camera, not surveyed dimensions. Drawing perspective is inconsistent; the full image match remains open. The hidden elevation retains the archetype's reconstructed treatment.

window_w_m.note: Reconstructed 0.75 m sash width under the provisional drawing camera, revised from the first rendered 0.55 m estimate. Cameron supplies the relative visible arrangement, not a measured window width. The selected width and retained 0.95 m height remain reconstructed pending the full comparison.

window_h_m.note: The visible sash is approximately half the doorway's height in Cameron's retrospective picture. 0.95 m follows the reconstructed 1.95 m doorway and remains a provisional proportion, not a measured historic dimension. The pictured occurrence/proportion bounds this choice, but its metric dimensions depend on reconstructed openings/eave height; the numeric attribute is therefore reconstructed.

door_w_m.note: Reconstructed 1.45 m doorway width under the provisional drawing camera, revised after the first rendered 0.85 m door read too narrow. The depicted dark opening bounds its appearance, without supplying an independent metric scale. A closed generic door remains a visible difference from the pictured open doorway.

door_h_m.note: Initial doorway height used to scale the pictured sash. The picture contains no independent scale; 1.95 m retains the archetype's approximately human-height opening rather than asserting a historic measurement.

end_openings.note: Cameron's visible gable has one small framed opening above its log wall, approximately centred. It is assigned to the local +x gable for the reference-view comparison; this is a model-frame choice, not a compass bearing supplied by the picture. The generator's 0.7 by 0.8 m light and its initial 3.35 m centre height are reconstructed within the existing roof. This uses a framed light rather than loft:true, which builds a closed boarded hatch. The pictured occurrence/proportion bounds this choice, but its metric dimensions depend on reconstructed openings/eave height; the numeric attribute is therefore reconstructed.

chimney_ridge_at.note: The one visible chimney rises through the roof rather than standing against an exterior gable. Its initial station is 0.6 of the ridge from the local minimum-u end, estimated from the retrospective drawing and awaiting rendered comparison. Neither an exact station nor the stack's dimensions are attested. The pictured arrangement is the visual bound; its exact station remains a reconstruction pending a solved comparison.

chimneys.note: One stack is visible above the roof in Cameron's retrospective picture of the post office in 1833. This supports an inferred visible count, not a scene-date attestation or a finding about hidden stacks. chimney_ridge_at states its provisional position; ridge_stack_w_m states a reconstructed section while the head and construction retain the archetype's treatment, recorded in docs/LIBERTIES.md L-hogan-pictured-openings-2377 and L26.

ridge_stack_w_m.note: Reconstructed 0.65 m square ridge-stack section, reduced from the generic 0.96 m after comparing the actual render to Cameron's narrower visible stack. This numerical section and unseen plan depth are not measured from the retrospective drawing. The archetype's 0.95 m head and plain cap remain reconstructed; masonry/cap details remain unmatched.

function.note: NOT THE POST OFFICE AT THE SCENE DATE, which is the fact this record exists to get right. It held Chicago's first post office from 31 March 1831 until about July 1834, when Andreas has the office removed to near the corner of Franklin and South Water, where it stayed through Hogan's term. What the building was doing on 1835-07-01 is NOT ATTESTED: it is recorded as a store because that is what it was before the post office arrived ('a log house occupied as a store') and alongside it for three years, and because nothing describes it changing to anything else. Brewster, Hogan & Co. advertised as forwarding and commission merchants in the early numbers of the Chicago Democrat, but no source reached puts the firm in THIS building in 1835, so the record carries no occupants block rather than guessing at one. THE STORE IS NOW ATTESTED IN HOGAN'S OWN WORDS, AND SO IS THE READING THIS ATTRIBUTE EXISTS TO GET RIGHT. Three printings of the Chicago Democrat in August and September 1834 — after Andreas has the post office removed — carry his standing card: "J. S. C. HOGAN, [O]FFERS at Wholesale and Retail, at his Store in South Water Street, one door belo[w th]e Post O[ff]ice, Dry Good[s], Grocer[i]es, [H]ardware, Cr[oc]kery and Gl[ass] W[a]re" (1834-09-03, page 3 column 6, claim chicago_democrat_1834_09_03#c023, dateline '[J]uly 30, 1834'; the same advertisement runs 1834-08-13 page 3 column 5 claim #c017 and 1834-08-20 page 3 column 5 claim #c007, both cut at the direction word). A fourth card, 1834-03-25 page 3 column 3 claim #c010, has him selling 300 cedar posts. So a wholesale and retail store on South Water Street is documented in the year before the scene date, which is what this attribute claims, and the value stays 'store'. THE POST OFFICE IS A FINDING AND IT IS RECORDED RATHER THAN ACTED ON. Hogan places his store 'one door below the Post Office' from August 1834, which is exactly the period this record has the office already removed 'to near the corner of Franklin and South Water' — and one door is not four blocks. Both cannot be true as written. NOTHING IS MOVED ON THE STRENGTH OF IT: the register's own bound is that a placement inference never displaces a committed documented building and a conflict is a finding, not a nudge (T-0196). The candidates are that Andreas's removal is later or nearer than he says, that Hogan's card is standing copy carried over from before the removal (its dateline of 30 July 1834 is within weeks of it), or that this record's reading of Andreas is too precise. Filed for the register to adjudicate against the 1835 file, which is where a scene-date fixture for Hogan already exists. THE READING IS TRANSCRIPTION-MEDIATED AND SAYS SO. Under the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 a claim read through this project's OCR-assisted transcriptions rather than off the page scan grades `attested` in this schema's vocabulary while carrying its own flag: reading = transcription_mediated, with the transcription's own uncertainty brackets preserved inside the quotation rather than tidied away. Where a scan is later read, the scan is the authority and this claim upgrades under it — the standard data/sources/chicago_democrat_1833_11_26.json set when a scan caught 'C. & I. HARMON' where the transcription had 'C. & L. Harmon'.
